sections.heading: Introduction to Child Custody Laws
sections.content: Child custody and guardianship in Bangladesh are primarily governed by the personal religious laws of the parties involved, alongside statutory laws like the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, and the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985. The most fundamental principle guiding the courts, overriding all other rules, is the "welfare of the minor." While personal laws prescribe specific rules regarding who gets custody at what age, the Family Court has the ultimate authority to decide custody arrangements based on what is in the best physical, moral, and psychological interest of the child. sections.heading: Muslim Law: Hizanat (Custody) and Wilayat (Guardianship)
sections.content: Under Muslim Personal Law, there is a distinct difference between custody (Hizanat) and guardianship (Wilayat). The mother has the primary right to Hizanat—the physical care and upbringing of the child. For a son, this right lasts until he reaches the age of seven. For a daughter, the mothers right continues until she attains puberty. However, the father is always considered the natural and legal guardian (Wali) of the child, responsible for the childs financial support, education, and property, even while the child is in the mothers physical custody. sections.heading: When Can a Mother Lose Custody Rights?
sections.content: The mothers right to Hizanat is not absolute. She may lose this right under specific circumstances outlined in Muslim law and interpreted by the courts. Common grounds for a mother losing custody include if she marries a person not related to the child within the prohibited degrees (a stranger), if she leads an immoral life, if she neglects the child, or if she resides far away, making it difficult for the father to exercise his guardianship duties. sections.heading: Fathers Rights and Responsibilities
sections.content: The father, as the natural guardian, has the right to custody once the mothers period of Hizanat ends (after 7 years for a boy, and puberty for a girl). Even during the mothers custody, the father retains the right to supervise the childs upbringing and has an absolute obligation to provide maintenance. If the mother is disqualified or passes away, the custody right typically passes to the maternal grandmother, and then to other female relatives, before eventually coming to the father. sections.heading: The Role of the Family Court
sections.content: When parents separate and cannot agree on custody, a suit must be filed in the Family Court under the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985. The judge assesses various factors: the financial stability of the parents, their moral character, the childs attachment, and the childs own preference if they are old enough to form an intelligent opinion. The court can grant interim custody orders during the pending trial. The court also establishes visitation rights, ensuring the non-custodial parent has regular and meaningful contact with the child to maintain their relationship. sections.heading: Non-Muslim Custody and the Guardians and Wards Act
sections.content: For citizens belonging to other religions, and in matters not strictly covered by personal law, the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 applies. This Act provides a comprehensive framework for appointing guardians of both the person and the property of a minor. Hindu law generally recognizes the father as the natural guardian, followed by the mother. Christian and other personal laws also have specific provisions, but across all communities in Bangladesh, the secular principle of the "welfare of the minor" remains the supreme guiding doctrine for the judiciary. sections.heading: Modifying Custody Orders and Legal Aid
sections.content:
Custody orders are not necessarily permanent; they can be modified by the court if there is a significant change in circumstances that affects the childs welfare. For example, if the custodial parent plans to move abroad, or if the childs needs change drastically as they grow older, a new petition can be filed. Navigating child custody disputes is emotionally draining and legally complex. It requires sensitive handling and expert legal representation to protect the parents rights and, most importantly, the childs future.

faqs.question: Can a father get custody of a child under 7 years old?
faqs.answer: Generally, Muslim law gives custody of a child under 7 to the mother. A father can only get custody if he proves the mother is unfit or disqualified under the law, prioritizing the childs welfare.

faqs.question: Does a mother automatically lose custody if she remarries?
faqs.answer: Under traditional Muslim law, marrying a "stranger" (someone not closely related to the child) can disqualify a mother. However, courts now often rule that if the remarriage does not negatively affect the child, she may retain custody.

faqs.question: Can the court consider the childs preference?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the child is old enough and mature enough to form a reasonable opinion, the Family Court judge will speak to the child and consider their preference, though it is not the only deciding factor.

faqs.question: Who pays for the childs maintenance after divorce?
faqs.answer: Under law, the father is legally obligated to provide maintenance (food, clothing, education, medical expenses) for the child, regardless of who has physical custody.
